paras: The attempted lynching at Marion, Ohio, was a mob's effort to lynch an unnamed Black man on a Sunday evening in mid-1903, known only from a passing reference in an Atlanta Constitution editorial. The editorial gave no outcome, accusation or name, and used the episode to rebuke a Northern critic of Southern lynching.

According to the Constitution, the attempt took place on the same Sunday evening on which an Ohio ex-federal general walked out of a public meeting of a "recent convention" in Atlanta, after a speaker said something about lynching in the South. The editorial said that the next morning the general read in the Constitution that "a mob at Marion, in his own state of Ohio," was trying "to lynch a negro man" at that very moment. It did not give the date, the size of the mob, what the man was accused of, or whether he survived.
The Constitution's original news report of the Marion mob does not appear in the coverage, and no Ohio paper or Black newspaper account was found.
No report of arrests, an inquest or any official response appears in the coverage.

The Atlanta Constitution printed the reference on July 20, 1903, in an editorial headed "Some Coincidences," which called the timing "a very sad coincidence" and paired it with the burning of a Black man by a West Virginia mob, reported just as the paper received a book by a West Virginia Republican legislator attacking "the south's treatment of the negro." The editorial's point was the hypocrisy of Northern critics rather than the Marion mob itself, which it neither condemned nor defended.

The editorial circulated beyond Atlanta: the Monroe City Democrat in Missouri reprinted it on July 23 with credit to the Constitution, and the Guthrie Daily Leader in Oklahoma ran it in full on July 27. No Black newspaper coverage of the Marion attempt was found.

reader.title: Attempted lynching at Marion, Ohio (1903)
bases: The only report describes a mob's 'endeavor to lynch a negro man' at Marion, Ohio, with no outcome given (A2).

The editorial reports only an attempt ('endeavor to lynch') by 'a mob' and does not say whether anyone was killed, how large the mob was, or what it accused the man of (A2). Without the underlying news report, the standard definition cannot be applied.

Everything rests on one passing reference in an Atlanta Constitution editorial to the paper's own earlier report (A2); A3 and A4 are reprints of that editorial, and the original news item was not found.

accounts.label: Atlanta Constitution editorial
accounts.gist: Says that, according to the Constitution's own report the next morning, a mob at Marion, Ohio, was trying to lynch a Black man on the Sunday evening an Ohio general walked out of an Atlanta meeting over remarks on lynching.

framing.detail: The Constitution's 'Some Coincidences' cites the Marion mob ironically ('a very sad coincidence, wasn't it?') to turn Northern condemnation of Southern lynching back on an Ohioan; it neither condemns nor defends the mob itself.
The Monroe City Democrat and the Guthrie Daily Leader reprinted the editorial with credit to the Atlanta Constitution and without comment.
